newsitem.title: USA: DuPont to cut 2,850 jobs in $750 million restructuring.
newsitem.headline: DuPont to cut 2,850 jobs in $750 million restructuring.

text.p: DuPont Co. said Thursday it will cut about 2,850 jobs in a $750 million restructuring aimed at rejuvenating its huge nylon fiber business.

The diversifed conglomerate said it expects to invest $150 million annually to implement the five-year programme, which is expected to reduce costs by $700 million a year and raise returns to well over the cost of capital.

DuPont Nylon is the Wilmington, Del.-based company's largest chemicals and specialities business, with revenues from fibers, chemicals and engineering plastics in excess of $5 billion. DuPont Nylon has 28 manufacturing sites worldwide.
About 15 percent of the business' 19,000 jobs worldwide will be reduced within three to four years, the majority through normal attrition, it said.

DuPont said it will modernise plants and equipment, consolidate the production of carpet, apparel and industrial nylon at fewer sites and improve efficiency in processing nylon fiber. It will also improve sourcing by taking better advantage of the global scope of its operations.

"Successful implementation of our renewal plan will clearly allow us to grow revenue and earnings much faster globally," said Ed Van Wely, vice president and general manager of DuPont's global nylon business.
The plan "will enable us to radically improve our flexibility and responsiveness in an increasingly dynamic and competitive marketplace," he said.

State-of-the-art nylon spinning technology will replace selected existing equipment beginning in 1997, DuPont said, explaining that it would enable increased capacity at greatly reduced capital and fixed cost.

The new technology significantly improves quality in areas such as product uniformity and dyeability and enables introduction of a steady stream of new, differentiated products with make-to-order flexibility, DuPont said.
The renewal "will more than double the shareholder value of the business by 2002," Van Wely said.

"The value of the renewal programme is enhanced by its integration with our strong intermediates technology and market position. We're continuing to modernise and expand existing intermediate facilities in Europe and North America, and we're generating new intermediates capacity with our Singapore plant and our joint venture with BASF in Asia."

DuPont's stock edged up 62.5 cents to $93.125 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday. The stock fell Wednesday on market talk that the company would not spin off its Conoco energy unit, traders said.

Wall Street has speculated on a Conoco spinoff after the company said in June that it was restructuring the business and had been in talks with Phillips Petroleum Co. on combining refining, marketing and transportation operations.
